newsitem.title: RWANDA: FEATURE - School is Rwanda's grisly memorial to genocide.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - School is Rwanda's grisly memorial to genocide.

text.p: From a distance Murambi school in Rwanda looks deserted. The stench is the only sign that something is wrong. Returning pupils would find their classrooms filled with thousands of corpses.
The school in the remote town of Gikongoro, 170 km (110 miles) southwest of the capital Kigali, is now an official museum of the country's 1994 genocide.
The exhibits are bodies of thousands of slaughtered Tutsis and moderate Hutus, exhumed from nearby mass graves.
"I've been to Auschwitz a couple of times, but it doesn't even come close to this," a young American soldier said.

Room after room is packed with corpses, strewn across the cement floors in a mess of limbs, skulls and torsos. Skin is bleached, flesh desiccated, the bodies shrivelled into caricatures of human beings, the faces unrecognisable.
Scraps of clothing survive. Among the hundreds of dead men, women, children and babies the one spot of colour is a faded red pull-over, far too big for the toddler who was killed wearing it.

"The Gikongoro memorial will be the first in the country," Gikongoro's deputy mayor in charge of social affairs told journalists visiting the hilltop site. "It is the only one where we have succeeded in digging up whole bodies."

The genocide was sparked by the assassination of Hutu military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994. Angry Hutu followers, soldiers and militia took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and Hutus politically opposed to Habyarimana.

An estimated 800,000 people were slaughtered across the country. The bloodshed was only ended three months later when the Rwandan Patriotic Front's (PRF) then rebel forces drove the Hutu army into exile in Zaire and Tanzania and took power.

In what looks like an assembly hall, workers in white coats and masks kneel beside a body. Painstakingly they brush and powder them for preservation, as calmly as paleontologists examining fossils in the backroom of a natural history museum.
Behind them decomposed clothing hangs on lines. Plastic bowls hold piles of skulls, the only reliable way to count how many died.
Local Police Chief Gilbert Rwampungu says they have recovered 25,000 bodies at the site and that is only half the total.
BODIES PROPERTY OF RWANDAN GOVERNMENT
Although most Rwandans in the ethnically divided Central African nation are unwilling to talk openly about the museum, it is clear not everybody agrees it is a good idea.
The dead are effectively the property of the government. Soldiers of the Tutsi-led PRF armed with assault rifles and grenade launchers stand guard on the hill.
One aid worker based in Kigali said: "One of the women in my office was terribly distraught as she was not able to get back the body of her husband. It was just taken away in a truck."
General Paul Kagame, Rwanda's vice-president and military leader, backs the museum, saying it is the best means to prevent history repeating itself.

"The way to deal with genocide is not by telling people to switch off and forget," said Kagame, a Tutsi who led the PRF to victory three years ago and is effectively in charge although Rwanda has a Hutu president.
"It will serve as a good memorial for what happened and to understand what happened," the soft-spoken general told reporters after a visit to the museum.
Playing down suggestions that relatives of the victims objected to the museum, he said there had been discussions at many levels.
"Finally we have moved forward on what should be carried out for the best of our country. It is fair to those that died and those that remain," he added.
When the massacres started, Hutus in the police and administration used public address systems to tell terrified Tutsis they would be safe at Murambi school.

After thousands of families had left their scattered farms to mass on the hilltop, Hutu soldiers attacked with automatic weapons, rockets and grenades over three days after April 19, 1994. The locals used machetes to finish off the few survivors.

One man escaped by hiding under a body, feigning death even as his shoes were stolen by his attackers. Now acting as a guide, he points out the bodies of his parents, who will be among those preserved to form part of a permanent monument.

While international attention is partly turned to the U.N. courtrooms in Tanzania where defendants accused of orchestrating the killing stand trial, the Murambi museum will ensure the memory of the victims remains fresh.
But some foreign workers say there is a danger that the museum will make reconciliation between Hutus and Tutsis harder. Forgiveness or remorse will be impossible while the dead remain unburied.

Standing by a room full of little corpses, Rwampungu explained how the small children were killed. "They were separated from their parents during the massacre, then someone said they should kill the babies too," he said.

Officials at the school suggested it might be re-opened one day, with the memorial transferred elsewhere. Perhaps a new generation of school children will visit the museum. The lessons they draw might help determine Rwanda's future.
